name: Business Law
notes: Competency areas come from the FBLA 2025-26 Business Law (High School) guidelines, updated Aug 2025: https://www.cteresource.org/media/xukjaoit/2526-business-law-va-fbla.pdf (copy of the FBLA guideline). Format: 50-minute online test, 100 multiple-choice questions, no deduction for wrong answers. The nine knowledge areas are the guideline's own list. The guideline's per-area percentage chart could not be read from the PDF text layer, so per-area question counts (15/20/10/10/15/10/10/5/5) are an approximation. Questions are original; law is U.S. (UCC, federal statutes, common law).
subs: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Which branch of the U.S. federal government has the main power to enact statutes?
choices: The regulatory branch of an executive agency
questions.explain: Congress enacts statutes. Courts interpret them, the executive enforces them, and agencies make regulations under delegated authority.

questions.q: Which element of a valid contract is the bargained-for exchange of value between the parties?
questions.explain: Consideration is something of legal value given in exchange for a promise. Capacity, legality and genuine assent are separate elements.

questions.q: An agent's authority that arises from the principal's conduct, leading a third party to reasonably believe the agent has power to act, is called:
questions.explain: Apparent authority rests on the third party's reasonable belief caused by the principal's conduct. Implied authority is actual authority inferred from the agent's duties.

questions.q: Which type of property is generally movable and not attached to land, such as furniture or a car?
questions.explain: Personal property is movable. Real property is land and things permanently attached to it, and fixtures are items that have become part of the land.

questions.q: Under the UCC, which warranty arises automatically when a merchant sells goods, even if the contract never mentions a warranty?
questions.explain: The implied warranty of merchantability attaches to sales by merchants of goods of the kind sold. Express warranties must be stated by the seller.

questions.q: Which dispute resolution method uses a neutral third party whose decision is binding on the parties?
questions.explain: Arbitration produces a binding decision by a neutral arbitrator. Mediation and conciliation help parties reach their own agreement and are not binding.

questions.q: In a partnership where some owners have limited liability and at least one owner has unlimited liability, the business is a:
questions.explain: A limited partnership has at least one general partner with unlimited liability and limited partners whose liability is capped. A general partnership gives every partner unlimited liability.

questions.q: A written, unconditional order by one party directing a second party to pay money to a third party is called a:
questions.explain: A draft has three parties (drawer, drawee and payee). A promissory note is a promise to pay made by the maker and involves only two parties.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Which document lets a person name an agent to handle financial matters if the person becomes incapacitated?
questions.explain: A durable power of attorney survives the principal's incapacity. A living will addresses end-of-life medical care, not finances.

questions.q: Which federal law makes it a crime to access a computer without authorization or to exceed authorized access?
questions.explain: The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (1986) is the main federal anti-hacking statute. The DMCA addresses copyright protection technology.

questions.q: A court's obligation to follow precedent from earlier decisions on similar facts is known as:
questions.explain: Stare decisis means to stand by things decided. Judicial review is the power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

questions.q: Which contract must be in writing to be enforceable under the Statute of Frauds?
choices: A contract for the sale of $400 of goods
A contract that can be performed within one year
A contract for cash services paid upfront
A contract for the sale of land
questions.explain: Contracts for the sale of land fall under the Statute of Frauds. Goods sales require a writing only at $500 or more under UCC 2-201.

questions.q: Which event ends an offer by operation of law?
choices: The offeree accepts on the stated terms
The offeror says the offer stays open for 30 days
The offeree asks a question about delivery
The death of the offeror before acceptance
questions.explain: An offer ends by operation of law on the death or incapacity of either party before acceptance. Acceptance forms a contract, and a question is not a counteroffer.

questions.q: An employee injured on the job generally receives benefits from which program?
questions.explain: Workers' compensation is a no-fault system funded by employers that pays benefits for work-related injuries. Unemployment insurance covers job loss.

questions.q: Which easement lets a landowner cross a neighbor's land to reach a public road when the land is otherwise landlocked?
questions.explain: An easement by necessity arises when a parcel has no access to a road. An easement by prescription arises from open, continuous, adverse use over time.

questions.q: The party who brings a civil lawsuit is called the:
questions.explain: The plaintiff starts a civil suit. The defendant responds to it, and a prosecutor represents the government in criminal cases.

questions.q: On a promissory note, which party is the maker?
choices: The party to whom payment is promised
The party who must present the note for payment
The party who promises to pay
The party who transfers the note by endorsement
questions.explain: The maker is the primary party who signs a promise to pay. The payee receives payment, and endorsers transfer the instrument.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: A contract whose existence and terms are inferred from the parties' conduct rather than their words is:
questions.explain: An implied-in-fact contract is found from conduct. A quasi-contract is implied in law by the court to prevent unjust enrichment and is not based on agreement.

questions.q: Which federal law regulates the collection of debts by third-party debt collectors?
questions.explain: The FDCPA limits abusive and deceptive collection practices by third-party collectors. TILA governs credit cost disclosures.

questions.q: Under Subchapter S, a corporation's income and losses are:
choices: Taxed at the corporate level only
Passed through to shareholders and reported on their personal returns
Taxed at both the corporate and shareholder levels
Exempt from federal income tax entirely
questions.explain: An S corporation avoids entity-level federal income tax by passing items through to shareholders. A C corporation is taxed at the entity level and again on dividends.

questions.q: A tenant renting an apartment for a fixed term of one year holds which type of estate?
questions.explain: An estate for years is a leasehold with a fixed start and end date. A tenancy at will has no fixed term.

questions.q: Under respondeat superior, an employer is liable for an employee's torts when the employee:
choices: Acts entirely outside the employer's business
Commits the tort within the scope of employment
questions.explain: Respondeat superior makes employers liable for torts committed within the scope of employment. Independent contractors generally do not create that liability.

questions.q: A software license that lets users copy, modify and redistribute code on the same terms is commonly called:
questions.explain: Copyleft licenses require derivative works to carry the same open terms. Shrink-wrap, site and proprietary licenses restrict redistribution.

questions.q: A holographic will is a will that is:
choices: Witnessed by two people and recorded
Handwritten and signed by the testator
questions.explain: A holographic will is entirely in the testator's handwriting and signed. Many states accept holographic wills without witnesses, but the handwriting must be proven.

questions.q: Which area of law addresses wrongs against society that the government prosecutes?
questions.explain: Criminal law addresses offenses against society, prosecuted by the state. Civil and tort law address disputes between private parties.

questions.q: A court order requiring a party to perform the exact promised act is:
questions.explain: Specific performance compels the promised act and is used when money damages are inadequate, such as for unique goods or land.

questions.q: Advertising a product at a very low price with no intent to sell it, then pressuring buyers toward a costlier item, is:
questions.explain: Bait and switch is a deceptive practice. Loss-leader pricing is a real sale of a discounted item, and puffery is harmless exaggeration.

questions.q: Which form of business is a separate legal entity that offers owners limited liability?
questions.explain: A corporation is a separate legal entity, so owners' personal liability is generally limited to their investment. The other forms do not provide this.

questions.q: To be negotiable under the UCC, an instrument must be payable:
choices: On demand or at a definite time
questions.explain: UCC 3-104 requires payment on demand or at a definite time, among other elements. Payment that depends on an uncertain event defeats negotiability.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: A relationship in which one party authorizes another to act on its behalf and under its control is:
questions.explain: Agency is created when a principal authorizes an agent to act for it under the principal's control. A bailment concerns temporary possession of goods.

questions.q: A legal claim against property to secure payment of a debt is called a:
questions.explain: A lien is a claim on property that secures a debt. An easement is a right to use land, and a covenant is a promise about land use.

questions.q: Which law gives electronic signatures the same legal effect as handwritten signatures in interstate commerce?
questions.explain: The Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce (E-SIGN) Act gives electronic signatures and records legal effect. The others regulate financial privacy, corporate reporting and telemarketing.

questions.q: Which court typically hears appeals and reviews the trial record for legal errors rather than retrying the facts?
questions.explain: Appellate courts review for legal error and generally do not retry facts or hear witnesses. Trial courts decide facts.

questions.q: Besides offer and acceptance, what must be present for a contract to be enforceable?
questions.explain: Enforceable contracts generally require offer, acceptance and consideration. Notarization and recording are not general requirements.

questions.q: A written agreement made before marriage that sets out how property will be divided is a:
questions.explain: A prenuptial agreement is made before marriage and governs property and support. A separation agreement is made after the couple decides to live apart.

questions.q: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, covered non-exempt employees must receive what pay for hours worked over 40 in a workweek?
choices: Double pay for all hours worked
Overtime pay of at least 1.5 times the regular rate
Paid time off equal to hours worked
questions.explain: The FLSA requires at least time-and-a-half for hours over 40 in a workweek for non-exempt employees. Other options are not federal requirements.

questions.q: A holder in due course takes a negotiable instrument free of most defenses. Which of the following is still a valid defense against such a holder?
choices: The holder paid full value in good faith
The holder took the instrument by a qualified endorsement
The instrument was payable to bearer
questions.explain: Forgery is a real defense that survives holder-in-due-course status. Good faith value, a qualified endorsement and bearer status are all features of HDC status or negotiability, not defenses.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Which federal act requires lenders to disclose the finance charge and annual percentage rate on consumer credit?
questions.explain: TILA requires standardized disclosure of credit costs, including the finance charge and APR. The other laws cover credit reports, lending discrimination and debt collection.

questions.q: A process in which a neutral person helps the parties reach their own agreement but cannot impose a decision is:
questions.explain: A mediator facilitates a voluntary settlement and cannot impose an outcome. An arbitrator decides the dispute.

questions.q: Which form of co-ownership gives the surviving owners the deceased owner's share automatically?
choices: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship
questions.explain: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship passes a deceased owner's interest to the surviving owners automatically. Tenants in common pass their shares through their estates.

questions.q: The corporate officer generally responsible for day-to-day management, who reports to the board of directors, is the:
questions.explain: The CEO runs daily operations and reports to the board. Shareholders own the company, and auditors examine its financial statements.

questions.q: Which contract is voidable rather than void?
choices: A contract for an illegal purpose
A contract made by a minor
questions.explain: A minor's contract is voidable at the minor's option. Contracts for illegal purposes and contracts lacking an offer are void.

questions.q: A principal is bound to a contract made with a third party by its agent when the agent had:
choices: Authority only if the contract is notarized
questions.explain: Principals are bound by acts within actual or apparent authority. Notarization is not a general requirement, and later-acquired authority does not bind retroactively.

questions.q: Which federal law limits the online collection of personal information from children under 13?
choices: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
questions.explain: COPPA requires parental consent and limits data collection for children under 13. HIPAA covers health records, and GLBA covers financial privacy.

questions.q: An endorsement consisting only of the endorser's signature on the back of an instrument is a:
questions.explain: A blank endorsement names no payee, so the instrument becomes payable to bearer. Qualified, restrictive and conditional endorsements add words or limits.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Under TILA, which right lets a consumer cancel certain loans secured by the principal dwelling within three business days?
choices: Right of withdrawal under the FCRA
questions.explain: The TILA right of rescission applies to certain home-secured credit transactions such as refinancing. The FCRA does not give a cancellation right, and setoff and subrogation are unrelated remedies.

questions.q: The doctrine requiring a party to have a sufficient personal stake in a case to bring it is:
questions.explain: Standing requires a concrete injury tied to the defendant's conduct. Mootness and ripeness concern timing, and venue concerns the proper place for trial.

questions.q: Which intellectual property right protects a new and useful machine design?
questions.explain: Patents protect new, useful and non-obvious inventions. Trademarks protect brand identifiers, and copyrights protect creative works.

questions.q: Which worker is most likely an independent contractor rather than an employee?
choices: A cashier paid hourly and supervised by a manager
A driver on set shifts using a company vehicle
A freelance designer who sets her own hours, uses her own tools and is paid per project
A factory worker enrolled in the company health plan
questions.explain: Control over hours, tools and method points to independent contractor status. Hourly pay, supervision and benefits point toward employment.

questions.q: A merger that combines companies in unrelated businesses is a:
questions.explain: A conglomerate merger joins firms in unrelated industries. A horizontal merger joins competitors, and a vertical merger joins firms at different stages of the same supply chain.

questions.q: Which is a common no-fault ground for divorce?
questions.explain: No-fault divorce is generally based on irreconcilable differences or an irretrievable breakdown of the marriage. Fault grounds such as adultery are not required and are not used in every state.

questions.q: Presentment for acceptance is required for which type of instrument?
choices: A promissory note payable on demand
A draft payable a fixed number of days after sight
questions.explain: Under UCC 3-501, a draft payable a fixed number of days after sight must be presented to the drawee for acceptance, which fixes its maturity. Demand instruments and certificates of deposit do not require acceptance.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Which practice is deceptive under FTC rules?
choices: Offering a clearly stated money-back guarantee
Claiming a product is clinically proven without supporting evidence
Listing cash and financing prices separately
Disclosing a product's country of origin
questions.explain: Advertising claims must be truthful and substantiated. The other options are lawful disclosure or guarantee practices.

questions.q: Which body decides whether there is enough evidence to bring a felony indictment?
questions.explain: A grand jury hears evidence and decides whether to indict. A petit (trial) jury decides guilt or innocence at trial.

questions.q: Which doctrine lets a court exercise personal jurisdiction over an out-of-state online seller that targets customers in the forum state?
questions.explain: Long-arm statutes and minimum-contacts analysis allow personal jurisdiction over nonresident defendants who purposefully reach the forum. Venue concerns the location of trial, and res judicata bars relitigation.

questions.q: Which document transfers title to real property?
questions.explain: A deed conveys title to real property. A lease grants possession, a mortgage secures a loan, and a bill of sale transfers personal property.

questions.q: An agent who purports to contract for a principal that does not exist is typically personally liable under the:
questions.explain: An agent impliedly warrants having authority, so misrepresenting a principal's existence exposes the agent to liability. The other doctrines do not address this situation.

questions.q: Which body is elected by shareholders to oversee corporate management?
questions.explain: Shareholders elect the board of directors, which oversees management. Officers are appointed by the board to run daily operations.

questions.q: A promise to keep an offer open for 30 days, made without payment or other consideration, is generally:
choices: Revocable by the offeror before acceptance
Binding because it was in writing
questions.explain: Without consideration or a separate option contract, a promise to hold an offer open is revocable before acceptance under common law. Writing and notarization do not supply consideration.

questions.q: Which document names someone to make health care decisions if the principal cannot communicate?
questions.explain: A health care proxy appoints an agent for medical decisions. A will governs property at death, and a codicil amends a will.

questions.q: Which standard of proof applies in a typical civil case?
questions.explain: Civil cases generally require a preponderance of the evidence, meaning more likely than not. Beyond a reasonable doubt is the criminal standard.

questions.q: Under strict product liability, a manufacturer may be liable for a defective and unreasonably dangerous product:
choices: Only if the buyer signed a warranty
Only if the seller and manufacturer are the same party
questions.explain: Strict liability focuses on the product's condition, not the manufacturer's fault. Plaintiffs need not prove negligence.

questions.q: Which insurance principle limits recovery to the actual loss suffered?
questions.explain: The indemnity principle restores the insured to the pre-loss position without profit. Underwriting decides whether to insure, and the premium is the price paid.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: A contract provision that ends a party's duties automatically when a specified event occurs is a:
questions.explain: A condition subsequent terminates an existing duty when an event happens. A condition precedent must occur before a duty arises.

questions.q: A mechanic's lien is a claim against:
choices: Real property, for unpaid labor and materials that improved it
questions.explain: A mechanic's lien secures payment for work or materials that improved real property. It attaches to the property itself.

questions.q: Which federal law prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin?
choices: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
questions.explain: Title VII prohibits employment discrimination on those five bases. The ADEA covers age, the ADA covers disability, and the Equal Pay Act covers pay differences by sex.

questions.q: A combination in which one company absorbs another, and only the absorbing company survives, is a:
questions.explain: In a merger, the surviving company absorbs the other. In a consolidation, both companies cease to exist and a new company is formed.

questions.q: Which filing gives public notice of a creditor's security interest in personal property under the UCC?
questions.explain: A UCC-1 financing statement perfects a security interest in most personal property. Deeds of trust and mortgages secure real property.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Which federal agency polices unfair or deceptive trade practices?
questions.explain: The FTC enforces the FTC Act's prohibition on unfair and deceptive practices. The SEC regulates securities, and the Federal Reserve oversees monetary policy and banks.

questions.q: A party signs a contract after being told a false fact that induced the signing. This defense is:
questions.explain: Fraudulent misrepresentation makes a contract voidable when a party relies on a knowingly false material fact. Duress involves threats, and undue influence involves a dominant relationship.

questions.q: Which requirement must be met for a federal court to hear a state-law claim under diversity jurisdiction?
choices: Complete diversity of citizenship and more than $75,000 in controversy
Both parties reside in the same state
The federal government must be a party
The claim must arise under a federal statute
questions.explain: Diversity requires complete diversity among parties and an amount in controversy above the statutory threshold, currently $75,000. Federal-question cases need a federal claim.

questions.q: A doctrine excusing performance because an unforeseen event made it impossible is:
questions.explain: Impossibility of performance excuses a duty when an unforeseeable event, not the party's own choice, makes performance impossible. Anticipatory repudiation is a breach.

questions.q: Which employer duty is required under the Occupational Safety and Health Act?
choices: Providing a workplace free from recognized serious hazards
Offering paid vacation after one year
questions.explain: OSHA requires employers to protect workers from recognized serious hazards. It does not set wages, vacation or unemployment coverage.

questions.q: A bailment is created when:
choices: Title passes permanently to a buyer
A landlord leases land to a tenant
Possession of personal property is temporarily transferred and must be returned
A debtor pledges real estate as collateral
questions.explain: A bailment transfers possession, not title, and the bailee must return or dispose of the goods as agreed. Title transfer, leases and real estate pledges are different arrangements.

questions.q: Charging an interest rate above the legal maximum on a loan is called:
questions.explain: Usury is charging interest above the lawful limit. Redlining is discriminatory lending, amortization is repayment scheduling, and escrow holds funds for a third party.

questions.q: Which is the highest court in the U.S. federal court system?
questions.explain: The U.S. Supreme Court is the highest federal court and the final appellate authority on federal questions. Courts of appeals and district courts are lower federal courts.

questions.q: Which contract term describes a claim that a contract cannot be enforced in court because a required writing is missing?
questions.explain: An unenforceable contract is valid between the parties but cannot be enforced, such as one lacking a required writing. A void contract has no legal effect.

questions.q: Which fiduciary holds property for another's benefit under a written trust instrument?
questions.explain: A trustee holds legal title and manages property for beneficiaries under a trust instrument. A bailee holds goods temporarily, and a surety guarantees another's debt.

questions.q: Which business form combines limited liability for owners with pass-through taxation and fewer formal requirements than a corporation?
questions.explain: An LLC gives owners limited liability and can be taxed as a partnership, with fewer formalities than a corporation. A franchise is a licensing arrangement, not an entity type.

questions.q: Under UCC 2-207, between merchants, an additional term in an acceptance generally:
choices: Becomes part of the contract unless it materially alters it or the offer limits acceptance to its terms
Must be notarized to take effect
questions.explain: Between merchants, additional terms usually become part of the contract unless they materially alter it, the offer forbids them, or objection is made. Notarization is not required.

questions.q: Which of the following is a duty an agent owes to the principal?
choices: Acting as guarantor for third-party debts
Loyalty and disclosure of material information
Providing unlimited credit to the principal
questions.explain: Agents owe fiduciary duties of loyalty, obedience and disclosure to the principal. The other options are not agent duties.

questions.q: Which party to a check is the drawee?
choices: The bank on which the check is drawn
The person who writes the check
The person who receives the check
The person who endorses the check
questions.explain: The drawee is the bank that must pay the check. The drawer writes it, and the payee receives it.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Which federal statute regulates consumer credit reports?
questions.explain: The FCRA governs the accuracy, privacy and use of consumer credit reports. The other statutes address electronic transfers, product packaging and telemarketing.

questions.q: A promise to make a gift with nothing given in return is generally:
choices: Enforceable because it is in writing
Enforceable under the Statute of Frauds
Enforceable only if the promisor is a corporation
questions.explain: A gratuitous promise lacks consideration and is generally unenforceable. Writing does not supply consideration.

questions.q: Which defense applies when a party is forced to sign a contract under threat of physical harm?
questions.explain: Duress is coercion by threats that overcome a party's free will, making the contract voidable. Undue influence arises from a relationship of trust.

questions.q: Under the parol evidence rule, which statement is correct?
choices: It allows oral evidence to override any written term
It applies only to oral contracts
It requires contracts to be notarized
It generally bars prior or contemporaneous oral terms that contradict a fully integrated written contract
questions.explain: The parol evidence rule protects integrated written agreements from contradiction by earlier or contemporaneous oral terms. Exceptions exist for fraud, ambiguity and certain terms.

questions.q: Which promise must be in writing under the Statute of Frauds?
choices: A promise to pay the debt of another if that person defaults
A promise to deliver flowers next week
A promise to pay for a meal today
questions.explain: Promises to answer for another's debt, called suretyship promises, must be in writing. The other promises can be performed quickly or are gifts.

questions.q: A mutual mistake supports rescission when:
choices: One party was careless in reading the terms
The buyer simply regrets the contract later
Both parties were mistaken about the same material fact at formation
The mistake concerns future market prices
questions.explain: Mutual mistake about a material fact existing at formation can justify rescission. Carelessness, regret and mistakes about future prices do not.

questions.q: Which remedy cancels a contract and returns the parties to their pre-contract positions?
questions.explain: Rescission cancels the contract and restores the parties. Specific performance compels performance, and reformation rewrites the contract.

questions.q: Which contract defense covers terms that are grossly unfair and oppressive, often because of unequal bargaining power?
questions.explain: Unconscionability permits a court to refuse enforcement of grossly one-sided terms. Duress, accord and satisfaction, and novation are different doctrines.

questions.q: Which type of authority is expressly stated by the principal?
questions.explain: Express authority is granted in words, orally or in writing. Implied authority is inferred from duties, and apparent authority comes from the principal's conduct toward third parties.

questions.q: Under the FLSA, which employee is typically exempt from overtime?
choices: A retail stock clerk paid hourly
A cashier paid by the hour
A bona fide executive earning a qualifying salary
questions.explain: Bona fide executive, administrative and professional employees who meet salary and duty tests are exempt from overtime. Hourly workers are generally non-exempt.

questions.q: Which law requires employers to provide unpaid, job-protected leave for certain family and medical reasons?
choices: Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act
questions.explain: The FMLA provides up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for qualifying reasons. The other statutes address pay equity, minimum wage and mass layoffs.

questions.q: Which property interest is a right to use another's land for a specific purpose without owning it?
questions.explain: An easement is a non-possessory right to use land for a specific purpose. Fee simple and life estates are ownership interests, and tenancy by the entirety is a form of co-ownership.

questions.q: Which legal form of business has unlimited personal liability for the owner and is the easiest to form?
questions.explain: A sole proprietorship requires no formal filing, and the owner is personally liable for business debts. The other forms involve formal filings or limited liability.

questions.q: Which corporate action creates a new company from two merging companies, which both cease to exist?
questions.explain: In a consolidation, the combining companies cease to exist and a new entity is formed. In a merger, one company survives.

questions.q: Which type of endorsement limits further negotiation, such as one that says 'For deposit only'?
questions.explain: A restrictive endorsement limits how the instrument may be used, such as requiring deposit only. A special endorsement names a payee, and a qualified endorsement disclaims liability.
questions.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

questions.q: Which principle requires that a court have authority over the type of dispute being heard?
questions.explain: Subject-matter jurisdiction is the court's authority over the kind of case. Personal jurisdiction concerns the parties, and venue concerns the location.

questions.q: Which concept requires that laws give fair notice and fair procedures before the government deprives someone of life, liberty or property?
questions.explain: The Due Process Clauses require fair procedures before deprivation. Equal protection concerns unequal treatment, and judicial review and stare decisis concern courts' roles.

questions.q: Which term describes a court's power to review whether a law violates the Constitution?
questions.explain: Judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison, lets courts strike down unconstitutional laws. Stare decisis is the rule of following precedent.

vocab.def: An alternative dispute resolution process in which a neutral arbitrator hears the case and issues a binding decision.
A non-binding process in which a neutral mediator helps disputing parties reach their own voluntary settlement.
The process of resolving a dispute through the court system.
The doctrine that courts should follow the precedents set by earlier decisions in similar cases.
The requirement that a party have a sufficient personal stake and injury to bring a lawsuit.
A court's legal authority to hear the type of case presented.
A group of citizens that hears evidence in private and decides whether there is probable cause to indict.
The constitutional guarantee that the government must follow fair procedures before depriving a person of life, liberty or property.
Something of legal value, such as a promise, act or forbearance, bargained for and exchanged in a contract.
A rule requiring certain contracts, such as those for land or suretyship, to be evidenced by a signed writing to be enforceable.
A rule that generally bars prior or contemporaneous oral agreements from contradicting a fully integrated written contract.
A defense allowing a court to refuse enforcement of a contract term that is grossly unfair and oppressive.
A remedy that cancels a contract and restores the parties to their pre-contract positions.
A court order requiring a party to perform exactly what the contract promised.
A doctrine excusing a party's duty to perform when an unforeseeable event makes performance impossible.
A contract that one party may choose to cancel, such as a contract made by a minor.
The failure of a party to perform a duty owed under an enforceable contract without a legal excuse.
A contract whose existence and terms are inferred from the parties' conduct and circumstances.
A business entity that gives owners limited liability and can be taxed as a partnership or corporation.
A corporation that passes income and losses through to shareholders for federal tax purposes if it meets eligibility rules.
A partnership with at least one general partner who has unlimited liability and limited partners whose liability is capped.
A transaction in which one company absorbs another, and only the surviving company continues to exist.
A combination in which two or more companies cease to exist and a new company is formed.
The group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation's management and major decisions.
The highest form of land ownership, which is unlimited in duration and transferable.
A leasehold interest that lasts for a fixed, definite period.
A non-possessory right to use another's land for a specific purpose.
A legal claim against property that secures payment of a debt or obligation.
A written instrument that transfers title to real property.
A temporary transfer of possession of personal property to another party, who must return or dispose of it as agreed.
A relationship in which an agent acts on behalf of and under the control of a principal.
Authority that a third party reasonably believes an agent has, based on the principal's conduct.
A doctrine making an employer liable for torts an employee commits within the scope of employment.
A worker who controls how the work is done and is not an employee for most legal purposes.
A duty of loyalty and care that an agent or trustee owes to the principal or beneficiary.
A no-fault system, funded by employers, that pays benefits for work-related injuries and illness.
The part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 that prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin.
A written, unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed sum of money that can be transferred by endorsement or delivery.

vocab.def: A holder who takes a negotiable instrument for value, in good faith and without notice of defects, and takes it free of most defenses.

vocab.def: A written order by a drawer directing a drawee to pay a payee, such as a check or bill of exchange.
vocab.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

vocab.def: An endorsement consisting only of the endorser's signature, which makes the instrument payable to bearer.
vocab.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

vocab.def: The demand for payment or acceptance of an instrument made by or on behalf of the holder.
vocab.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

vocab.def: A legal interest in collateral that secures a debt and gives the creditor rights in that property if the debtor defaults.
vocab.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

vocab.def: The insurance principle that limits recovery to the actual loss so the insured is not profited.
vocab.sub: Negotiable instruments, insurance, secured transactions, bankruptcy

vocab.def: A federal law requiring lenders to disclose standardized credit terms, including the finance charge and annual percentage rate.
A federal law that restricts abusive and deceptive debt collection practices by third-party collectors.
A deceptive practice of advertising a low-priced item with no intention to sell it, then steering buyers to a costlier one.
Charging interest on a loan above the maximum rate allowed by law.
Liability of a seller or manufacturer for a defective and unreasonably dangerous product, without proof of negligence.
An automatic UCC warranty that goods sold by a merchant are fit for their ordinary purpose.
An open-source license that requires derivative works to be distributed under the same terms as the original code.
A federal law that makes unauthorized access to protected computers a crime.
A state law allowing a court to exercise personal jurisdiction over nonresident defendants who have sufficient contacts with the state.
A federal law giving electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as handwritten ones in interstate commerce.
A contract made before marriage that sets out how property and support will be handled if the marriage ends.
A document appointing an agent to manage a person's financial affairs that remains effective if the person becomes incapacitated.
A will written entirely in the testator's own handwriting and signed by the testator.
A document appointing an agent to make medical decisions if the principal cannot communicate.
A written amendment to an existing will that must be executed with the same formalities as a will.
A divorce granted on grounds such as irreconcilable differences, without proof of marital misconduct.
